issues.legal_issue: Conversion of land into a plantation after the commencement of the ceiling provision does not qualify the converted land for exemption when determining the land to be surrendered.
material_facts: The landholders converted land into plantations after the ceiling provision had come into force.
They claimed that the plantations were exempt from the ceiling provisions.
issues.conclusion: The conversion must be disregarded when determining the extent of land liable to be surrendered, and the plantation exemption does not override that restriction.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 1(3), 81(1)(e) and 82(4) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 apply. Under section 1(3), a reference to the commencement of the Act in a provision means the coming into force of that provision; the amended section 82(4) therefore applied from the commencement of section 82. The plantation exemption in section 81(1)(e) is subject to section 82(4). The Court substantially approved Ramunni Nair v. State of Kerala and distinguished State of Kerala v. Philomina and State of Kerala v. K. A. Gangadharan.

predicates.ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding determines the land liable to be surrendered under a statutory landholding ceiling.
predicates.land_converted_into_plantation_after_cei: A landholder converted land into a plantation after the ceiling rule governing conversion had come into force.

issues.definition: When a ceiling proceeding concerns land converted into a plantation after the ceiling rule commenced, the conversion is disregarded in determining the land to be surrendered.

issues.legal_issue: A purchase certificate conclusively proves the assignment it records but does not prevent the ceiling authority from determining the extent and identity of excess land.
material_facts: A Land Tribunal could issue a certificate recording the assignment of a landowner's and any intermediary's rights to a tenant.

In ceiling proceedings, the Taluk Land Board was required to verify the landholder's statement, ascertain whether the holder owned or held other land, and determine the extent and identity of land to be surrendered.
The issue arose whether a purchase certificate bound the Board in those proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The Board must treat the certificate as conclusive proof of the assignment it records, subject to facial inaccuracy or fraud, but retains authority to determine the extent and identity of excess land and to make its own order.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 72K(2) and 85(1), 85(5) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 govern. Section 72K(2) makes the certificate conclusive proof only of the assignment of rights stated in it; it does not make findings on other matters conclusive or remove the Board's functions under section 85(5). The certificate cannot be disregarded merely because the Tribunal allegedly assessed evidence improperly or committed a procedural error; facial inaccuracy or fraud may be examined. The Court held that Kunjanujan Thampuran v. Taluk Land Board was not quite correct and relied on the general treatment of conclusive evidence described in Halsbury's Laws of England.

predicates.ceiling_board_proceeding: A land ceiling authority is determining the landholder's surplus land and the land to be surrendered.
predicates.purchase_certificate_submitted: A party submits a certificate recording the assignment of a landowner's and any intermediary's rights to a tenant.

issues.definition: When a purchase certificate is submitted in a ceiling-board proceeding, the authority must accept the recorded assignment as conclusive but may still determine the excess land.

issues.legal_issue: The clarification that the ceiling area for assessing specified voluntary transfers is the reduced ceiling applies to transfers made after publication of the land reform bill.
material_facts: The original transfer provision treated specified voluntary transfers made after publication of the bill as transfers calculated to defeat the Act and invalidated them.
A later amendment reduced the ceiling area.
A subsequent amendment clarified that the ceiling area referred to in the transfer provision was the area under the reduced ceiling.
The Court considered the validity of transfers made after publication of the bill by reference to the reduced ceiling.
issues.conclusion: The clarification operates retrospectively to require the validity of the covered transfers to be assessed against the reduced ceiling.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 82(1) and 84(1)–(3) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 apply. The Court construed the clear wording of section 84(3) in light of section 84's purpose of preventing transfers that defeat the ceiling scheme and the fact that the original provision already selected the bill's publication as the date from which transfers could be invalidated. A declaratory clarification may relate back to the earlier enactment. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. K. A. Gangadharan and approved Narayana Patar v. State of Kerala; it also referred to the principles of statutory construction and the treatment of declaratory statutes in Craies on Statute Law.

predicates.transfer_validity_proceeding: A proceeding determines whether a voluntary transfer is invalid under a statutory land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.voluntary_transfer_after_bill_publicatio: A landholder voluntarily transferred land after publication of the bill that proposed the ceiling scheme.
predicates.transfer_exceeds_reduced_ceiling: The transfer leaves the holding above the reduced ceiling applicable under the later amendment.

issues.definition: In a transfer-validity proceeding, a voluntary transfer made after publication of the bill is assessed against the reduced ceiling and is invalidated if it exceeds that ceiling.

issues.legal_issue: A child in the womb on the appointed date is not counted as a family member for calculating the additional ceiling area allowed for family members beyond the specified number.
material_facts: The ceiling calculation allowed additional land for each family member beyond a specified number.
The statutory definition of family included a husband, wife and their unmarried minor children, or such of them as existed.
The statutory definition of a minor depended on whether the person had attained the age of eighteen years.
The claimed additional allowance depended on counting a child who was in the womb on the appointed date.
issues.conclusion: A child in the womb on the appointed date is not counted as a family member for that ceiling calculation.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 82(1)(c), 2(14) and 2(36A) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 apply. The Court held that the member must be in existence and it must be possible to determine that the member had not attained eighteen years on the appointed date; those conditions are not met for a child in the womb. It approved the view in Balakrishna Kurup v. State of Kerala.

predicates.family_ceiling_calculation: A statutory ceiling is being calculated by reference to the number of members in a landholder's family.
predicates.claimed_member_was_unborn_on_appointed_d: A person claimed as a family member had not yet been born on the date fixed for calculating the ceiling.

issues.definition: In a family-based ceiling calculation, a person not yet born on the appointed date is not counted as a family member.

issues.legal_issue: A ceiling authority may revise its earlier determination to correct a mistake based on reports already on the record.
material_facts: The Taluk Land Board increased its earlier determination of excess land after taking account of reports that had been overlooked in the first determination.
The reports had been made by officers authorized to provide them.
The challenge was to the Board's authority to correct its earlier order.
issues.conclusion: The revision was permissible under the statutory power to set aside or revise the Board's earlier order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 85(9) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 permitted the Board to correct its earlier determination in the circumstances described. The Court also noted that section 105A(1) authorized the relevant officers to make the reports relied upon.

predicates.ceiling_board_proceeding: A land ceiling authority has determined the surplus land to be surrendered by a holder.
predicates.earlier_surplus_order_contains_overlooke: An earlier surplus-land determination overlooked a report already on the record that was made by an authorized officer.

issues.definition: A ceiling authority may correct an earlier surplus-land determination when it overlooked an authorized report already on the record.

issues.legal_issue: Transfers made after the date on which the ceiling obligation becomes operative must be disregarded when determining the landholder's liability, even if they fall within a category of transfers otherwise excepted from invalidation.
material_facts: Landholders made gift transfers after the date on which the ceiling obligation became operative.
The transfers were claimed to be of a kind excepted under the transfer provision.
The Taluk Land Board and High Court did not exclude the gifted land from the ceiling determination.
issues.conclusion: The transfers were to be ignored in determining liability to surrender excess land, even if they were of an otherwise excepted variety.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 83, 84 and 85 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 apply. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. K. A. Gangadharan, which held that transfers made after the operative date are to be ignored for the ceiling determination even when they are of an excepted variety mentioned in section 84.

predicates.ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding determines a holder's liability to surrender land exceeding a statutory ceiling.
predicates.transfer_made_after_ceiling_obligation_b: The landholder transferred land after the statutory ceiling obligation became operative.

issues.definition: In a ceiling proceeding, land transferred after the ceiling obligation became operative is ignored when determining the land to be surrendered.
